Messages.Author: Simon
Messages.Body:
Ok, in the scenario:
Muddled VH vs some vampire.
vampire wants to play a strike: dodge card.

Does First Strike mean the damage hits before the dodge can be played?
or does that dodge work for First strikes too?

If Strike: Dodge _does_ stop 1st strike, then can it also be used to block the
strike from 'Strike: Dodge with additional strike' off twisted Acrobatics?

please clarify. At the mo the MVH minces us lot unless we have twisted auspex

thanks in advance
Simon

Messages.Author: James R. McClure Jr.
Messages.Body:
ch...@mail.bris.ac.uk (Simon) wrote:
>
> Ok, in the scenario:
> Muddled VH vs some vampire.
> vampire wants to play a strike: dodge card.
>
> Does First Strike mean the damage hits before the dodge can be played?
> or does that dodge work for First strikes too?
>
> If Strike: Dodge _does_ stop 1st strike, then can it also be used to block the
> strike from 'Strike: Dodge with additional strike' off twisted Acrobatics?

Peace Simon,

The order of strike resolution is:
Dodge (that is, a dodge cancels (sp) the opposing strike [not
Strike: End Combat tho'])
First Strike
Strike (that is, 'normal' speed strikes come last)
The answer to your first question is, "Yes, you may dodge a first strike."

No, Strike: Dodge can only stop an Additional Strike if played by a vampire
also taking Additional Strikes. This makes AddStrikes quite nasty. If
your opponent plays sup Acrob [Strk:Dodge w/ AddStrk] and you don't have
Celerity, your strike is ineffective and you will take the AddStrk and can't
Dodge it [hope you brought some Fortitude].

Nil carborundum illigitimi,

James R. McClure Jr.
The OS/2 Apostle

Messages.Author: Stephen Beaulieu
Messages.Body:
In article <D7ED...@info.bris.ac.uk>, ch...@mail.bris.ac.uk (Simon) wrote:
> Does First Strike mean the damage hits before the dodge can be played?
> or does that dodge work for First strikes too?
>
> If Strike: Dodge _does_ stop 1st strike, then can it also be used to
block the
> strike from 'Strike: Dodge with additional strike' off twisted Acrobatics?

The current ruling is that a dodge will dodge any strike (except a combat
ends) during the strike resolution phase in which it is played. So, a
dodge will dodge a first strike from a MVH (or any other for that matter)
It does not dodge an additional strike. Superior acrobatics gives an
additional strike, creating an additional strike resolution phase. To
have a strike during this phase you must also have additional strikes.
Now, there is nothing to stop you from dodging additional strikes if you
have more dodges to play at that time.

hope this helped.
stephen

Dodge beats First Strike.

>If Strike: Dodge _does_ stop 1st strike, then can it also be used to block the
>strike from 'Strike: Dodge with additional strike' off twisted Acrobatics?

In order to stop the second strike, you'd have to have a second
strike of your own. Dodge only provides a cancellation of one strike,
and you'd need to play another one during the additional strike phase to
stop the additional strike.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Simon <ch...@mail.bris.ac.uk> wrote:
>Muddled VH vs some vampire.
>vampire wants to play a strike: dodge card.
>Does First Strike mean the damage hits before the dodge can be played?
>or does that dodge work for First strikes too?

Like "combat ends", "dodge" takes effect as soon as it is played,
so kicks in before a first strike would.

>If Strike: Dodge _does_ stop 1st strike, then can it also be used to block the
>strike from 'Strike: Dodge with additional strike' off twisted Acrobatics?

No. Dodge just neutralizes a strike with respect to the dodging minion.
It does not neutralize other aspects of the strike, so the additional
strike will be produced, dodging a Burst of Sunlight will still result
in the other minion taking damage, and so on.

Tom Wylie rec.games.trading-cards.* Network Representative for
aa...@cats.ucsc.edu Wizards of the Coast, Inc.

Or, better, just Leave It Alone (TM). Sudden Reversal Cancels a Master
Card. Dodge and Combat Ends both cancel strikes, whether with first
strike or not. The fact that they (should) resolve after first strike
doesn't change the fact that they cancel the strike with first strike.

If the DT keeps screwing with the timing, then pretty soon, were going to
have a stack of instant effects with little whirlpools of interrupts to
resolve. I don't think anybody wants that.

Request for DT: Munchkinize Mt$. Let the vampires alone.

>If the DT keeps screwing with the timing, then pretty soon, were going to
>have a stack of instant effects with little whirlpools of interrupts to

The Jyhad/V:TES design team is making a conscious effort to avoid timing
issues. They (we?) don't want Jyhad to have the timing baggage that
Magic does. But I don't really see how having combat ends work immediately
is timing baggage; Sudden Reversal is certainly much closer to a real
timing issue than combat ends is.

Messages.Body:

>Magic does. But I don't really see how having combat ends work immediately
>is timing baggage; Sudden Reversal is certainly much closer to a real

It's timing baggage because it takes the rules and changes how
they are applied. It takes the way you'd expect things to work and
turns them around. Suddenly this card precludes you playing a card,
which isn't something the rules cover. Sudden Reversal, at least,
mentions that it's futzing with cardplay. The DT has made CE futz with
cardplay without any rules reason. A little bit here, a little bit
there, and suddenly we have timing rules...

Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3o3bs8$2...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>,

Thomas R Wylie <aa...@cats.ucsc.edu> wrote:

>That would make a fair amount of sense, true, but dodges are basically
>seen as a diluted version of Combat Ends, which we very definitely want to
>take effect right away, rather than waiting for any strike resolution step.
>As long as there's one strike that takes effect right away, there's no
>real harm in having two.

But there's real harm in having *any* strike that takes effect
right away. If you have cards that deny other players the chance to
play cards, especially when the rules don't even imply such a thing is
possible, you break those portions of the game that those denials
affect. Jyhad shouldn't have the ability to play a card curtailed.
Doing so gives a great advantage to the person who can stop cards from
being played.
*Please* stop this trend before it starts and reverse the ruling
on Combat Ends. Let it resolve normally. It will still have the *same*
effect on combat, and won't have undesirable cardplay side effects.

Forward this to the design team, or whatever. Just don't
continue down this course, for the sake of the game.



That's your perspective. Back up for a moment. Until the DT
issued the ruling that CE was instantaneous, everyone here on the net
and everyone I played with locally played it such that CE was resolved
during strike resolution. From *our* perspective you *did* change the
way it was played.
The best example I can think of is the clockwork ruling from
Magic. Most people interpreted it one way and the DT interpreted it
another. Same thing has happened here.

I formally ask the design team to consider this ruling again,
taking the common interpretation into account, much as the Magic team
did for the clockwork ruling. Would you please forward this request to
the Design Team, Tom? Thank you.

Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3o69sl$c...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>,

Thomas R Wylie <aa...@cats.ucsc.edu> wrote:

>Joseph Cochran <js...@discus.ise.vt.edu> wrote:
>> But there's real harm in having *any* strike that takes effect
>>right away. If you have cards that deny other players the chance to
>>play cards, especially when the rules don't even imply such a thing is
>>possible, you break those portions of the game that those denials affect.
>
>Do you have a problem with Day Operation? It stops anyone from
>playing any kind of card that would involve blocking the vampire, after all.

But Day Operation specifies on the card that you can't stop it,
and there's *still* the opportunity to play other reactions. Card play
is not denied, merely hindered. And it's spelled out. The CE ruling is
not based on something that spells out card denial, and it hoses all
possible cards that the opponent could play at that moment, especially
if you forbid master cards in combat (which you have said that you do).
This denial is not laid out anywhere that any reasonable person will see
in the rules, and is non-intuitive, especially given the wording in the
rules which says "considered a strike" with *no* other qualifiers
indicating instantaneous effect nor card denial. It is nowhere near Day
Operation (which, I might add, is also balanced out by being a rare
while CE is common in many cases).

>The rules should not have to say you can always (or never) stop people from
>being able to play cards. If a card or sequence of play allows others to
>play cards, then fine; and if it doesn't, that's fine too.

But the rules *should* indicate where likely places are that
will stop you from playing cards. Day Op fits the bill fine, because it
does specify what will happen. The CE ruling doesn't, because it is the
opposite from what a reading of the rules will give you.

>> *Please* stop this trend before it starts and reverse the ruling
>>on Combat Ends. Let it resolve normally. It will still have the *same*
>>effect on combat, and won't have undesirable cardplay side effects.
>
>The design team does not find the way combat ends works to be undesirable.
>We consider it to be just fine.

It is a counterintuitive ruling. It adds new paragraphs to
the rules out of whole cloth. It adds a very bizarre side effect to the
card that I cannot see any reason to support (please tell me *why* you
feel that CE must deny card playing). That alienates your players and
frankly, makes you look like you haven't played the game (I know that
you have, and I know that you as a team are experts, but that *is* the
impression others have stated here in the group). Much like in the
clockwork ruling from Magic, you interpret it differently from everyone
else on the net, and probably most of those not on the net, too.

To paraphrase Fagin: I think you better think it out again.



>not based on something that spells out card denial, and it hoses all

>possible cards that the opponent could play at that moment...

Day Operation largely hoses any cards your opponents might be interested
in playing. Sure, they can use Telepathic Counter if you're bleeding them
via the Day Operation, but they can't do anything if you're equipping
with a weapon. Combat ends does not completely deny playing cards; they
could still play Psyche, for example. It just so happens that Day Operation
is typically used on actions like bleeding, which do have reactions that
don't involve trying to block the vampire, but in essense it severely hinders
the opponent's ability to react, so isn't terribly different from
combat ends in that regard.

>This denial is not laid out anywhere that any reasonable person will see
>in the rules, and is non-intuitive, especially given the wording in the
>rules which says "considered a strike" with *no* other qualifiers

What else is "this ends combat immediately" (description of combat ends)
supposed to mean? If it was supposed to end combat during Resolve Strikes,
why would we say "immediately"?

We can argue back and forth based on the rulebook all day, and we all know
the rulebook is unclear or inaccurate in many cases. But you can certainly
get the "blocking minion can't even strike" interpretation out of the rules
given for combat ends.

Yes - as soon as the vamp announces it (in the LARP, this
is just done by a quick arm motion) I back down. When it's
announced, it's turned on.

: When a vamp hits me with claws, I take a point of agg damage - but not until

Why the same with Majesty? Again, thinking first of the RPG and the LARP,
it *is* the thought that counts. You're only going to lay your
wolf claws on that Prince if you can blindside him (in Jyhad
game mechanics, deny him a strike).

The reason I bring up the RPG and LARP is that the only things that
bug me about the game are things that are broken and things that
are not consistent with the RPG. Fixing a game problem by ruining
part of the connection with the RPG is not acceptable either.

The DT ruling on Majesty
makes sense in the context of the RPG; it does feel a bit broken, but
unless I'm completely missing some point, I don't see any way
that having it resolve in the Strike Resolution makes a significant
difference. Unless...

Is your preferred interpretation that, if Majesty *is* resolved
during strike resolution, that the other vamp can actually have their
strike resolved as well? If yes, I disagree with it even more. It's
the whole idea of the Presence discipline - you're so impressive that an
opponent won't get close enough to lay a finger on you. To cut to the
chase, tell me what having Majesty resolve during strike resolution
would really fix, and how...my guess is that either it doesn't fix
much, or it makes Jyhad move away from how Presence is conceived
of in the RPG/LARP. In either case, my reaction is negative.

But still the same amount of blood (Majesty requires payment of
one blood for an untap). Depends on what kind of deck you're
playing whether this distinction is really important or not.
Blood in my pool is more valuable than blood on my vamps, but
is spending 4 pool + 1 card worse than spending 4 blood off of
vamps and spending 4 cards (and having a large number of dupes
in my deck and in my hand)? It's not so clearcut then...at
least to me. Especially if I'm playing with lots of titled
vamps, minion taps, blood dolls...in which case their blood is
my blood to some extent.

Messages.Author: Alan Kwan
Messages.Body:
The game rules on card playing sequence during combat has nothing to
do with the actual sequence of the occurence of actions that playing
those cards simulates. The acting minion does not in any way act first
simply because he gets to play a strike first. The card playing order
is nothing more than a technicality to avoid the problems of
simultaneous declarations and allows for a more streamlined game play.
The order in which things actually happen is determined by the
rules concerning strike resolution (Combat Ends > Dodge > First
Strike > normal Strike).

If the acting minion can stop the blocking minion from doing anything
by waving his arm, why can't the blocking minion do the same to the
acting minion? The only logical explanation is that the timing of
the _play_ of a strike card has nothing to do with when the effects
occur; the effects occur when the strike _resolve_, after both players
have played a strike.

: prevent the acting vamp from playing a card. This is inconsistant.

If all this is only about the fact that a Majesty from a blocking
vampire from playing a pointless strike (ie, allowing the blocking
player to discard a strike card), then my reaction is that this
is all making mountains out of molehills. Anyway, isn't there
another general principle in the game, that you can't just toss
cards out when they are guaranteed to be pointless (such as,
burning stealth modifiers on an action before the blocker has
even come up with sufficient intercept)? Seems like what you
folks want to see with the Combat Ends strike is inconsistent with
that...

Even if you have Majesty resolve during strike resolution, I think
you still have to do some stuff that's outside of the rules as
written. My recollection is that there is no timing or ordering
of the strikes in the resolution phase (except for first strike,
then regular)...So what in the rules would tell you that, if you
have two strikes to resolve (simultaneously), and one of them
is Combat Ends, the other strike would be ignored? Seems to me
that you have to extend the rules here to get the proper effect...
so from a rules purist point of view, I don't see that having the
strike resolve in the resolution phase is any improvement. Saying
that Combat Ends is first strike doesn't help, because what if the
blocker has first strike too?

It trades an asymmetry in strikes for a fuzzy area of rules.
Myself, I don't find the asymmetry in the strikes to be aesthetically
unpleasing, and it seems quite obvious how it works if it is
resolved when announced.

Sorry if this has been hashed over again and again already, but
I didn't see those discussions...and what I do see is a lot of
folks trashing the DT ruling and proposing something else, and
I see that something else as not fixing anything important and
being more ambiguous...
--
Jeremy (bea...@netcom.com, bea...@delphi.com)

A second majesty is not pointless.

"strike: dodge".

>have two strikes to resolve (simultaneously), and one of them
>is Combat Ends, the other strike would be ignored? Seems to me
>that you have to extend the rules here to get the proper effect...

No exceptions are needed. Each strike is well defined as to its effect
during resolution:

hands inflict one damage if at close.
lucky blow inflict two damage if at close.
.44 inflict two damage to opposing minion or any of his retainers.
steal blood move N blood from opposing vampire to yourself.

end combat end combat immediately, undoing effects of opponent's strike.

dodge cancel (undo) the effect of the opponent's strike on you.

any of these can resolve during the "first strike" phase if they are done with
first strike, and any will be cancelled by an appropriate "cancelling" strike
regardless of first strike.

After resolution, any damage done (agg or normal) to a vampire may be healed
if possible, and could send a vampire to torpor or the ashheap if sufficient
blood is not available to heal/prevent destruction (normal/agg, resp.).

Note that the "untap this minion" part of a card that ends combat is
(officially, even!) not part of the strike, but a separate effect provided
by the card.

>so from a rules purist point of view, I don't see that having the

>strike resolve in the resolution phase is any improvement. Saying
>that Combat Ends is first strike doesn't help, because what if the
>blocker has first strike too?

First strike is irrelevant to CE and to Dodge.

>It trades an asymmetry in strikes for a fuzzy area of rules.
>Myself, I don't find the asymmetry in the strikes to be aesthetically
>unpleasing, and it seems quite obvious how it works if it is
>resolved when announced.

Obvious if that is the case, yes. Obvious *why* that is the case, no.

>folks trashing the DT ruling and proposing something else, and

>: >player to discard a strike card), then my reaction is that this
>: >is all making mountains out of molehills. Anyway, isn't there

>: No, it's about allowing the blocker to End Combat and untap as well as
>: the attacker, or at least declare a strike, just like the attacker
>: gets to do.

>Ahh, ok, no one had mentioned this example before. I can understand

>the objections a bit better now...but I still don't see it as a big
>problem...just MHO...Hmm, trying to recall if Concealed Weapon is
>a strike card as well - that was about the only other constructive
>use of the strike I could think of...

No. Concealed Weapon is a combat effect that must be played before range
is determined.
And it is not a "big" problem until you play a Majestic bleed deck.
And it is never a "big" problem if you play it as a strike instead of
as an announce-strike effect. So the "big" problem argument falls against the
DTR.

>: No exceptions are needed. Each strike is well defined as to its effect
>: during resolution:

>: end combat end combat immediately, undoing effects of opponent's strike.

>I believe that "undoing effects" language is not in the rule book.

Yes, it is. Combat Ends... even Cancels a strike done with First Strike.

You can't cancel a strike that hasn't happened yet, and by the DTR,
the First Strike will not occur to be cancelled. It would've had to read
"even prevents a strike done with First STrike from occurring".

>That's what I was referring to when I said that having Combat Ends
>resolve during Strike Resolution requires you to extend the rules.

No extension from my POV.

>I could be mistaken, but I'm sure you'll correct me if that's the case.
>(Say, is there an on-line version of the Jyhad rulebook somewhere?
>I'd much rather refer to the real thing rather than my recollection)

I'll mail you a copy of the "Corrected" Rules.

>: Note that the "untap this minion" part of a card that ends combat is

>: (officially, even!) not part of the strike, but a separate effect provided
>: by the card.

>It seems to me that *this* is the source of the problem, and not

>the DT ruling...the untap ability is just too good, too cheap.

That, too. But at least that follows the rules and card text without
any hand-waving by the DT.

bea...@netcom.com (Jeremy York) wrote:
>James R. McClure Jr. (jrmc...@ulkyvm.louisville.edu) wrote:
>

>: It means that the reacting vampire may play cards, if for no other reason than

>: to attempt to cycle through his/her deck. Why should Majesty "freeze" your
>: opponent Meth's hand? No, even if Majesty (on any other CE for that matter)
>: resolves in Strike Resolution the opponent's strike has no effect. It also
>: has to do with consistancy, Jeremy. It is inconsistant for one strike to
>: act totally different from all other strikes. If the blocker plays CE, it doesn't
>: prevent the acting vamp from playing a card. This is inconsistant.
>

>If all this is only about the fact that a Majesty from a blocking
>vampire from playing a pointless strike (ie, allowing the blocking
>player to discard a strike card), then my reaction is that this
>is all making mountains out of molehills. Anyway, isn't there

>another general principle in the game, that you can't just toss
>cards out when they are guaranteed to be pointless (such as,
>burning stealth modifiers on an action before the blocker has
>even come up with sufficient intercept)? Seems like what you

>folks want to see with the Combat Ends strike is inconsistent with
>that...

Peace Jeremy,

There are at least two other occurances of "wasting" cards: acting vamp strikes to
Dodge - the blocking vamp may still strike; and during a vote - you may toss as many
Pol Actn cards as you have in your hand, even if they don't affect the vote. One
of the most important things that CE occuring "instantly" causes is it prevents the
blocking minion from playing a CE/untap also. This makes the CE/untap cards even more
powerful and I doubt that you would find any one here who feels that CE/untaps are
weak enough to need that boost.

>Even if you have Majesty resolve during strike resolution, I think
>you still have to do some stuff that's outside of the rules as
>written. My recollection is that there is no timing or ordering
>of the strikes in the resolution phase (except for first strike,
>then regular)...So what in the rules would tell you that, if you
>have two strikes to resolve (simultaneously), and one of them
>is Combat Ends, the other strike would be ignored? Seems to me
>that you have to extend the rules here to get the proper effect...

>so from a rules purist point of view, I don't see that having the
>strike resolve in the resolution phase is any improvement. Saying
>that Combat Ends is first strike doesn't help, because what if the
>blocker has first strike too?

No, Strikes have 'always' (since the revised rules) resolved in this order: 1) Combat
Ends, 2) Dodge, 3) First Strike, 4) normal Strike.

>It trades an asymmetry in strikes for a fuzzy area of rules.
>Myself, I don't find the asymmetry in the strikes to be aesthetically
>unpleasing, and it seems quite obvious how it works if it is
>resolved when announced.

So, you are saying that you don't feel the acting minion being about to CE/untap while
the blocking minion cannot is not a problem? Ever played against a Majestic bleed deck?

>Sorry if this has been hashed over again and again already, but
>I didn't see those discussions...and what I do see is a lot of
>folks trashing the DT ruling and proposing something else, and
>I see that something else as not fixing anything important and
>being more ambiguous...

We aren't proposing anything. DTR had said that strikes resolved as above. Recently
they altered that ruling to say that CE was instant. If it was supposed to work this
way, than why did they (DTR) put out an incorrect ruling? Why did it take so long to
fix? Why do most of the posters here find this to be a problem? And what about chair?
